To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Ca2+ binds to hCP in four distinct sites with different binding affinities, and that hCP is in its heterodimers form and at most half-bound with Ca2+ in resting cells, but is in its heterotetramer form and fully bound to Ca2+ upon release into the extracelluar environment.

hCP exists in the cytoplams of resting cells as an unbound heterodimer and, when released into the extracellular environment, binds four to eight Ca2+ ions and forms an oligomer that can bind and sequester essential transition metals from microbes.

Ca2+ binding to hCP is a two-step process in which the protein first binds Ca2+ ions in a 2:1 stoichiometry (hCP:Ca2+) that stabilizes the dimeric form, followed by binding of additional Ca2+ ions (1:2 stoichiometry, hCP:Ca2+), which stabilizes the tetrameric form of the protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the molecular details of Ca2+ coordination by the human calprotectin innate immune protein, a transition-metal-sequesting protein that is released from activated neutrophils into the extracellular environment.
the molecular mechanisms of Ca2+ regulation and the metal-withholding function in the innate immune system.
the development and application of MS methods that can be used to study metal binding to proteins in solution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ca2+ binding to hCP is a dynamic process, with the protein existing predominantly in a heterodimeric state and binding up to eight Ca2+ ions in a Ca2+-dependent and cooperative manner.
hCP exists as a Ca2+-free heterodimer in the cytosol, and that Ca2+-induced hCP oligomerisation occurs extracellularly.
hCP is a metal-withholding protein that is able to bind four Ca2+ ions per heterodimer, which is the minimum amount required for oligomerization to the functional tetramer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the integrated MS approach described in this work provides a robust and versatile tool to study metal-binding properties of proteins.
the integrated MS approach described here can be used to determine the stoichiometry and binding affinities for protein-metal and protein ligand interactions.
Ca2+ is a key regulator of hCP function and that the molecular details of its Ca2+ binding can now be understood in the context of its biological functions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the integrated MS-based approach can be readily applied to other protein-metal and/or protein-ligand binding interactions.

the MS-based methods used here can be readily applied to study other protein-ligand and protein-metal interactions, and that the integrated MS approach can be used to provide a comprehensive picture of protein-metal binding.
integrated MS methods provide a powerful means to elucidate protein-ligand interaction networks, including the stoichiometry and affinities associated therewith.
